text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The tax authority has simplified the routine for honest people who want to pay tax on services in their homes by allowing appropriate tax forms to be ordered over the phone.
The authority estimates that at least 10 billion crowns, possibly 15 billion, is paid annually for under-the-table work at peoples' homes.
- Derivatives trading exchange OM and the Stockholm stock exchange are working actively to merge.
- The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development forecasts steady growth for industrialised countries and average GDP of 2.5 percent per year until 1998.
- The paper's favourite computer games this year are Quake for action lovers and NHL 97 for hockey fanatics. The characters Emil and Finnish Mumi are popular in educational and story games.
- Swedish High Commander Owe Wiktorin has approved a request from Nato to use the Swedish force in Bosnia as a special unit.
If there is a crisis in Bosnia, the Swedish unit will be sent outside its designated area to be used as a kind of military fire squad or tactical reserve.

- OECD warns of Swedish wage inflation in its six-month Economic Outlook. The latest wage agreements led to higher salaries than the economy can take and they will cause Swedish export companies to lose market share over the next few years.

- Swedish exports keep going strong, but domestic order intake remains weak and the contruction market is nearly dead, according to the November report from Swedish government-controlled economic institute KI.

- The tentatively planned merger between the Stockholm Stock Exchange and the OM Group, which operates derivatives trading, is threatened by disagreement between two of their respective owners, the Wallenberg family and banking group Handelsbanken.
Handelsbanken leads a group of owners who opposes a merger solution that would give the Wallenbergs a dominating ownership position, newspaper sources say.

- Car safety equipment company Autoliv has achieved a breakthrough in Brazil through reaching an agreement with Ford's domestic subisidiary about delivieries of car safety equipment for three important models next year.

- Seven Swedish wooden house manufacturers have set up a joint venture to work on the Japanese market. Deregulation and support from Japanese authorities are boosting interest for foreign-made pre-fabricated wooden houses.
